When you call someone crotchety, you mean they are grumpy, irritable, and easily annoyed — but with an important extra layer: they also tend to hold odd, stubborn, and unreasonable opinions that they refuse to let go of. It's not just a bad mood. It's a settled habit of being difficult, contrary, and prickly about things.

Think of it as grumpiness + stubbornness + peculiar pet peeves, all rolled into one.
What a crotchety person actually does

A crotchety person:

  • Gets irritated by small, minor things that most people would simply ignore
  • Complains frequently, often about things that can't be changed or don't really matter
  • Holds fixed, sometimes bizarre opinions and refuses to be reasoned with
  • Resists change — new methods, new ideas, or new ways of doing things bother them
  • Is easily rubbed the wrong way, so people around them have to "walk on eggshells"
  • May snap or grumble at others without much provocation

For example, a crotchety neighbour might insist that the mail should always arrive before 10 a.m., and if it arrives at 10:05, they'll grumble about it for the rest of the day — even though it makes no practical difference to their life.

The "peculiar opinions" part — what makes it different from just "grumpy"

This is the key thing that separates crotchety from simply being grumpy or irritable.

A person who is just grumpy is in a bad mood or has a generally unhappy temperament.

A crotchety person, on top of that, has specific, often irrational little rules and opinions about how things should be — and they get disproportionately bothered when those rules aren't followed. These opinions might seem harmless but rigid, outdated, or just plain odd to everyone else. The person holds them very firmly and refuses to budge.

For example:

  • "Sandwiches must always be cut diagonally, never straight across."
  • "Young people today don't know how to write a proper letter."
  • "This new supermarket layout makes no sense. The old one was perfectly fine."

These aren't necessarily mean views — they're just oddly fixed, and the person gets genuinely annoyed when reality doesn't match them.
Who is usually described as crotchety?

The word is most commonly used to describe older people — a crotchety old man, a crotchety grandmother — though it can apply to anyone. The reason it's associated with older people is that the image it conjures is of someone who has grown rigid and set in their ways over time, someone whose tolerance for new things or minor inconveniences has worn thin.

It's worth noting that crotchety isn't used to describe someone in a single bad moment. It describes a personality trait or a pattern of behaviour — someone who is habitually like this.
The tone of the word — is it harsh or gentle?

Crotchety sits in a middle space. It is clearly negative — you wouldn't call someone crotchety as a compliment — but it isn't vicious or cruel. There's often a mildly affectionate or even slightly amused quality to it, especially when used about elderly people. It's the kind of word you might use about a relative or a well-known character in a story: you're not exactly defending their behaviour, but you're not condemning them harshly either. You're simply describing them as difficult, set in their ways, and a bit grumpy — in a way that's almost expected of them.

Compare this to a word like cruel, which is harsh and judgmental, or mean, which carries moral weight. Crotchety is more like a character quirk that people around the person have simply learned to live with.

• My grandfather gets crotchety if anyone touches the television remote without asking him first.
  • She's a brilliant editor, but she's become more crotchety with age and snaps at the junior writers over tiny mistakes.
  • The crotchety old professor refused to accept any assignment printed in anything other than Times New Roman.
  • Don't take it personally — he's crotchety with everyone in the mornings.
